title: Embodying the camera: An EEG study on the effect of camera movements on film spectators' sensorimotor cortex activation
authors: Heimann K, Uithol S, Calbi M, Umiltà MA, Guerra M, Fingerhut J, Gallese V
key_findings: Clips of an empty room filmed with a still camera, a zoom and a Steadicam move; beta-band mu-rhythm desynchronisation (motor-resonance marker) was stronger for Steadicam than for still or zoom clips
No equivalent modulation in occipital (attention) areas, which the authors read as a sensorimotor (not attentional) response
In post-session interviews participants described the Steadicam clips as the most realistic and most like a person approaching the scene; some felt they were walking toward the table
Participants: 18 right-handed adults (5 male, 13 female, mean age 24.3); 3-s clips, ~68-70 trials per condition
practical_applications: A physically moving camera (dolly/Steadicam/gimbal) reads as an embodied approach; a zoom of the same framing change does not - use dolly/push for 'the viewer steps closer', zoom for an optical, observing feel
Supports simulating a real camera translation (parallax) in 2D/2.5D rather than plain scaling when we want embodiment
limitations: Small sample, lab EEG, empty room, 3-s clips; mu suppression as a mirror-system index is debated (the paper cites Hobson & Bishop 2016)
Says nothing about liking, comprehension or retention

title: Moving Mirrors: A High-density EEG Study Investigating the Effect of Camera Movements on Motor Cortex Activation during Action Observation
authors: Heimann K, Umiltà MA, Guerra M, Gallese V
key_findings: (per search summary and Heimann2019's own summary) Compared a hand action filmed with a static camera vs a camera approaching the scene, and different ways of approaching; Heimann2019 reports the earlier study found approaching the scene with a camera modulated motor-cortex (mu) responses
practical_applications: Earlier evidence line for 'camera approach = bodily engagement' in push-ins on hands/products
limitations: Results not read directly; only abstract-level/secondary summary

title: The Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity
key_findings: Continuity editing works by cueing attention across the cut with natural cues: off-screen sound, conversational turns, motion onsets, gaze cues, pointing, exits from the field of view
Coinciding a cut with an attention shift minimises awareness of the visual transient; continuity can be kept without a coherent mental map of the depicted space

Explains match-action, matched exit/entrance, shot/reverse-shot, the 180-degree rule and POV editing; uses eye-tracking heat maps (e.g. Blade Runner 1982 gaze-cued cuts; an 'erroneous' shot/reverse-shot in Last Year at Marienbad)
The 30-degree rule 'jump' has been attributed to unintended apparent motion (Anderson 1996; Hochberg & Brooks 1978, cited)
practical_applications: Plan the camera position of shot B from where the viewer's eyes will be at the end of shot A (eye trace) - critical in 9:16
Use a look, a gesture or a sound to 'carry' the viewer across a cut or a camera move
limitations: Theory essay with demonstrations, not a controlled test of every rule; author's manuscript version read

title: Exploring the Effects of Violating the 180-Degree Rule on Film Viewing Preferences
authors: Kachkovski GV, Vasilyev D, Kuk M, Kingstone A, Street CNH
key_findings: Exp 1: naive viewers detect 180-degree violations (large effect)
Exp 2: violations can confuse/disorient viewers (relatively small effect)
Exp 3: violations did not change liking - viewers were as likely to prefer a version with a violation as one without
practical_applications: Keep the 180-degree rule for clarity of geography (it does reduce disorientation), but do not treat a deliberate crossing as fatal to enjoyment; use it when disorientation is the point
limitations: Short lab videos, student samples; enjoyment measured by preference, not long-form engagement

title: 180-degree rule
key_findings: Camera stays on one side of the axis between two characters so A is always frame-left of B; crossing = 'jumping/crossing the line'

Cites Frith & Robson 1975 and Magliano & Zacks 2011 for violations not impairing narrative understanding/memory of event order; Levin & Wang 2009 that spatial representations are not remembered across a movie
Lists deliberate violators: Dreyer (The Passion of Joan of Arc), Kubrick (The Shining bathroom scene), Godard (Breathless car scene), von Trier (Antichrist), Ozu, Wong Kar-wai, Tati
practical_applications: Pointer to primary literature and to film examples of deliberate line-crossing
limitations: Tertiary source; film examples are Wikipedia's, not verified in a scholarly source here

title: What Would Jaws Do? The Tyranny of Film and the Relationship between Gaze and Higher-Level Narrative Film Comprehension
authors: Loschky LC, Larson AM, Magliano JP, Smith TJ
key_findings: Hollywood-style film produces strong attentional synchrony - most viewers look at the same place at the same time - whether or not they had narrative context
Context improved comprehension (the critical inference) but changed gaze only slightly; results fit the 'tyranny of film' hypothesis better than the mental-model hypothesis
practical_applications: Framing, movement and editing steer the eye more than story knowledge does - the camera path must put the key object where the eye already is
limitations: One 12-s clip from a Bond film; abstract-level reading

title: Classifying cinematographic shot types
authors: Canini L, Benini S, Leonardi R
key_findings: Camera-to-subject distance strongly shapes the narrative (abstract)
Automatic classification of shots into three main scale classes using colour, motion distribution, spectral amplitude and content features
practical_applications: Shot scale is measurable from frames - basis for automated QC of shot-size variety in our clips
limitations: Only three coarse classes; abstract-level reading

title: CineScale: a dataset of cinematic shot scale in movies
authors: Savardi M, Kovacs AB, Signoroni A, Benini S
key_findings: (search summary) >792,000 frames from 124 movies annotated for shot scale; classes: ECU, CU, MCU, MS, MLS, LS, ELS, plus Foreground shot and Insert
practical_applications: Shows a 7-step scale plus 'foreground' and 'insert' is a workable research taxonomy - matches our SHOT_TYPE_LIBRARY steps
limitations: Only search snippet read; title/venue to be confirmed

title: The framing of characters in popular movies
key_findings: (abstract record) 48 popular films 1935-2010; number of characters on screen affects shot scale and shot duration; characters per frame declined roughly linearly over the years
Framing differs across aspect ratios, but character overlap is fairly constant once images are conformed to one shape
practical_applications: More characters in frame -> wider scale and longer shots; one character -> closer and shorter
limitations: Abstract-level; Art & Perception 3(2):191-212 per record

title: The evolution of pace in popular movies
key_findings: (search summary) 180 popular English-language films 1930-2015; shot duration, motion and luminance patterned across narrative acts; shots lengthen in the setup, shorten in parts of the climax
practical_applications: Shot size and movement intensity should follow the act structure: calmer/wider early, closer/faster toward the climax
limitations: Search-summary level for this module

title: Vection and visually induced motion sickness: how are they related?
authors: Keshavarz B, Riecke BE, Hettinger LJ, Campos JL
key_findings: Large field-of-view displays induce strong vection and tend to induce visually induced motion sickness (VIMS)
Adding viewpoint jitter to expanding optic flow increased both vection and VIMS (Palmisano et al. 2007, reviewed)
Multi-axis rotation produced more VIMS than single-axis rotation while vection stayed similar (Bonato 2009; Keshavarz & Hecht 2011a, reviewed)
Vection is not sufficient for VIMS; the relation remains unresolved
practical_applications: Shaky handheld + forward movement + roll at the same time is the riskiest recipe; keep FPV/handheld sections short and single-axis when possible, especially for full-screen phone viewing
limitations: Lab displays (drums, large screens), not phone video; read first ~2/3 of the full text

title: Motion parallax as an independent cue for depth perception
key_findings: (search summary) Random-dot displays showed motion parallax alone can specify 3-D shape and depth, both observer-produced and externally generated (as in film); observer-produced was more effective
practical_applications: Relative motion of layers (parallax) is a sufficient depth cue on a flat screen - the reason rig.js --d layers and 2.5D depth make still art feel 3-D
limitations: Only search summary/secondary reviews read

title: Calm that camera!
key_findings: Contemporary 'free camera' style is an intensification of classical continuity: nearly every shot moves independently of characters
Named tics: wobblecam, peekaboo reframing, arc / 'roundy-round' (term from director Ken Kwapis, used in E.R. for time slipping away), slider drift that promises a reveal that never comes

Fast cutting hides camera moves; Steadicam encouraged walk-and-talks; Bordwell values motivated movement that pays off pictorially (cites Ophüls, Mizoguchi, Die Hard) and finds gratuitous moves wasteful
practical_applications: Every move must pay off with a reveal or a change of relation; a lateral 'slider' drift with no reveal reads as filler
limitations: Scholar's blog essay (expert opinion, not empirical)

title: Film Art: An Introduction (13th ed.) - Ch. 5 'The Shot: Cinematography'
authors: Bordwell D, Thompson K, Smith J
key_findings: Part Three 'Film Style': Ch. 4 Mise-en-scene, Ch. 5 Cinematography (publisher listing)
13th edition expands digital filmmaking and streaming coverage
practical_applications: Standard academic taxonomy for framing (angle, level, height, distance) and mobile framing; cite for terminology
limitations: Chapter text not read this session (PDF behind captcha); only publisher page - older-edition content is summarised in visual-arts key BordwellThompson-FilmArt

title: The Five C's of Cinematography: Motion Picture Filming Techniques
key_findings: Organised around five areas: camera angles, continuity, cutting, close-ups, composition (publisher description); original Cine/Grafic 1965, 251 pp.
practical_applications: Classic checklist: every set-up is a choice of angle + its continuity + how it will cut + whether a close-up is earned + composition
limitations: Bibliographic/publisher description only; 1960s studio practice

title: Film Directing: Shot by Shot - Visualizing from Concept to Screen (25th Anniversary Edition)
key_findings: Michael Wiese Productions, 400 pp.; first ed. 1991; standard directing text on storyboarding, staging and camera choreography (bibliographic)
practical_applications: Reference for staging-in-depth and moving-camera choreography when planning camera paths
limitations: Content not read this session

title: Cinematography: Theory and Practice for Cinematographers and Directors (4th ed.)
key_findings: Routledge 2022, 528 pp.; TOC covers visual storytelling, the frame, lens language, continuity, shooting methods, cameras, exposure, colour, lighting, set operations (publisher page)
practical_applications: 'Lens language' and 'continuity' chapters are the craft backbone of FD04/FD05
limitations: Only TOC/publisher description read

title: Grammar of the Shot (4th ed.)
key_findings: Routledge 2017 (library records 2018), 308 pp.; covers shot composition, screen direction, depth cues, lighting, camera movement, shooting for editing, with exercises; a 5th edition exists
practical_applications: Basic shot-type naming and 'shooting for the edit' exercises
limitations: Publisher/catalogue description only

title: CameraCtrl: Enabling Camera Control for Video Diffusion Models (arXiv: ...for Text-to-Video Generation)
authors: He H, Xu Y, Guo Y, Wetzstein G, Dai B, Li H, Yang C
key_findings: Plug-and-play camera-pose module on top of a video diffusion model, driven by a parameterised camera trajectory; base model weights unchanged
Training data with diverse camera distributions and appearance similar to the base model improves controllability and generalisation; works with AnimateDiff, SparseCtrl, SVD; ICLR 2025
practical_applications: Text words alone are a weak camera controller; precise paths need pose/trajectory conditioning (not available in our Wan 5B setup) - so we plan paths as keyframes and fake them in HTML/2.5D, and use AI video only for the move it does reliably
limitations: Research system; abstract-level reading

title: MotionCtrl: A Unified and Flexible Motion Controller for Video Generation
key_findings: Controls camera motion and object motion independently via camera poses and trajectories ('appearance-free'); SIGGRAPH 2024
practical_applications: Camera move and subject move are separate channels - write them as separate clauses in prompts and plan them separately
limitations: Abstract-level reading

title: Towards Understanding Camera Motions in Any Video (CameraBench)
key_findings: ~3,000 internet videos annotated by experts; taxonomy of camera-motion primitives built with cinematographers; object-, ground- and camera-centric reference frames; includes follow/tracking, arcing, shaky steadiness, side-tracking

SfM methods miss semantic primitives that depend on scene content (e.g. follow); generative VLMs miss geometric primitives needing precise trajectories; expertise and tutorial training improve human annotation accuracy (NeurIPS 2025 spotlight)
practical_applications: Name a move in two layers: geometry (truck right 1 m) + semantics (following the walker). Train our own QC eye with a tutorial before judging moves
limitations: Search-summary/abstract level

title: Veo on Vertex AI video generation prompt guide
key_findings: Lists angles/shot types (eye-level, low, high, bird's-eye/top-down, worm's-eye, Dutch, CU, ECU, MS, full/long, wide/establishing, OTS, POV) with a note that some advanced angles aren't officially supported
Lists moves: static/fixed, handheld/shaky cam, whip pan, pan, tilt, dolly in/out, truck, pedestal, zoom (camera itself doesn't move), crane, aerial/drone, arc
Lens/focus: wide-angle, telephoto, fisheye effect, shallow/deep DOF, rack focus, lens flare, 'vertigo effect (dolly zoom)'
practical_applications: Vocabulary that a current commercial model is documented to accept
limitations: Undated page; docs moving to a 'Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform' path; acceptance != reliable execution
license: Google docs (CC BY 4.0 for content per Google default; unverified)

title: AI camera control (Runway resources article)
key_findings: Dated 2026-10-12; references Gen-4.5, Seedance 2.5, Veo 3.1, Kling 3.0
Prompt = move + speed + subject + reason ('Slow push-in on her face as she reads the letter'); multi-stage moves: describe what each stage reveals
For a still camera write 'locked' / 'mounted on a tripod' rather than 'static shot'; avoid 'following'/'revealing' which imply motion

One move per clip is most stable; don't let a preset and the prompt ask for different moves; set movement to zero in settings to stop unwanted motion; test short first for drift/edge warping/stalled moves
practical_applications: Direct rules for our AI-video prompt templates in CAMERA_MOVEMENT_LIBRARY
limitations: Vendor article (marketing context); model list will change

title: Gen-4 Video Prompting Guide (Runway help center)
key_findings: (search summary) 5 or 10 s from image + text; negative phrasing not supported and may give opposite results; separates scene motion from camera motion; points to a Camera Terms reference (Gen-4.5)
practical_applications: Never write 'no camera movement' - write 'locked-off tripod shot'
limitations: Page returned 403; snippet only

title: AI camera control guide (Kling quickstart)
key_findings: Six basic movements: horizontal, vertical, zoom, pan, tilt, roll; 'absolute commands' with adjustable displacement
Four Master Shots: move left and zoom in; move right and zoom in; move forward and zoom up; move down and zoom out
No ranges or model-version support listed on the page
practical_applications: Kling exposes camera as numeric axes - map our keyframe path to one axis per clip
limitations: No definitions/ranges; model versions not linked to the feature

title: Kling Camera Controls node (ComfyUI docs)
key_findings: Types: simple, down_back, forward_up, right_turn_forward, left_turn_forward

horizontal_movement (x translate, -left/+right), vertical_movement (y, -down/+up), pan = rotation in the vertical plane about x (-down/+up), tilt = rotation in the horizontal plane about y (-left/+right), roll (z, -ccw/+cw), zoom (focal length: negative narrows FOV, positive widens)
At least one value must be non-zero; not all model/mode combinations support camera control
practical_applications: WARNING: Kling's 'pan' and 'tilt' are swapped relative to film usage (Kling pan = up/down, tilt = left/right) per this doc - test with a 2-s clip before relying on it
limitations: Third-party integration doc; ranges not stated; third-party guides disagree on axes

title: Camera Concepts (Luma Dream Machine API changelog)
key_findings: 35 concept keys incl. static, handheld, pan_left/right, tilt_up/down, truck_left/right, pedestal_up/down, push_in, pull_out, zoom_in/out, crane_up/down, orbit_left/right, roll_left/right, dolly_zoom, aerial, aerial_drone, bolt_cam, tiny_planet, elevator_doors, selfie, pov, over_the_shoulder, low_angle, high_angle, overhead, ground_level, eye_level
API takes an array of concepts with model 'ray-2'
practical_applications: A ready vocabulary of move names a vendor trained on; keys double as our movement ids
limitations: Undated; old Dream Machine API superseded per curriculum ch.10 (Luma Agents API) - check before use

title: How to use camera motion (Luma learning hub)
key_findings: Pan = horizontal; orbit = rotate around a focal point for a 3-D effect; crane = vertical movement adding height/depth; push in/pull out described as 'zooms in or out' (conflates dolly and zoom)
Best use: bringing still images to life
practical_applications: Vendor vocabulary is loose - always add the physical meaning ('camera physically moves closer, background parallax')
limitations: Byline 2024-11-06 vs metadata 2026-11-18; terminology imprecise

title: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B model card
key_findings: Released 2025-07-28; 720P (1280x704 / 704x1280), 24 fps, 5-s clips; Wan2.2-VAE 16x16x4 compression
Training data includes 'detailed labels for lighting, composition, contrast, color tone, and more'
No explicit camera-control feature: camera is directed through the text prompt only; Apache 2.0
practical_applications: Our Wan setup: camera = prompt words only, one simple move, 480x848 on 6 GB (CAPABILITY_MATRIX)
limitations: Camera-word compliance not documented; must be tested

title: GSAP Eases documentation
key_findings: Default ease is power1.out; core eases none, power1-4, back, bounce, circ, elastic, expo, sine, steps
power1=quad, power2=cubic, power3=quart, power4=quint ('strong'); none = linear
practical_applications: rig.js cam.move defaults to sine.inOut, not GSAP's power1.out - always pass an ease deliberately
limitations: Software docs

title: Dolly zoom
key_findings: Dolly and zoom in opposite directions keep the subject's size while the background stretches/compresses; constant width W at distance d = W/(2 tan(FOV/2))

Credited to Irmin Roberts for Hitchcock's Vertigo; listed uses: Jaws 1975 (Brody's realisation), Goodfellas 1990, Poltergeist, Raging Bull 1980, The Lion King 1994 (Simba after the stampede), Fellowship of the Ring 2001, Shaun of the Dead 2004 (comic), Ratatouille 2007 (Ego's flashback)
Other names: Hitchcock/Vertigo shot, Jaws effect, zolly, trombone shot, contra-zoom
practical_applications: Use for a realisation/'world shifts' beat, once per piece; also works comically
limitations: Tertiary; film uses as summarised by Wikipedia

title: First shot using 'dolly zoom' (Guinness World Records) / Hitchcock-Truffaut account
key_findings: (search summary) Records the Vertigo (1958) shot as the first dolly zoom; names contra-, vertigo-, Hitchcock- or trombone-zoom; secondary sources report Hitchcock told Truffaut he had the idea on Rebecca and that second-unit cameraman Irmin Roberts devised the method
practical_applications: Historical attribution only
limitations: Not read in full; Truffaut interview not read directly

title: Steadicam / Garrett Brown
key_findings: (search summary) Invented by Garrett Brown, patent filed 1974; first feature use Bound for Glory (1976; some sources say 1975) - a crane shot that came down and Brown walked the camera through the set; used for Rocky's run up the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps
practical_applications: Historical anchor for 'Steadicam = floating embodied follow'
limitations: Dates disagree between sources

title: How cinematographer Roger Deakins & team pulled off the one-shot 1917 (MPA) / TheWrap / IndieWire coverage
key_findings: (search summaries) Deakins called the planning, not the shoot day, the real challenge; still frames of rehearsed blocking were turned into storyboards and schematics for grips/operators; Mendes and Deakins wrote 'a second script' for the camera movements; the 'one shot' is many long takes stitched; Alexa Mini LF; camera moved between rigs (e.g. shoulder to wire) mid-shot
practical_applications: Camera paths are written like a script: rehearse blocking first, then key frames, then the rig per segment - exactly the FD24 workflow
limitations: Press coverage, not read in full; the ASC article (theasc.com 'Lives Under Siege') only intro seen

title: Cooke Anamorphic/i (S35 2x, FF+ 1.8x, SF Special Flare) - Cooke Optics and trade coverage
authors: Cooke Optics; ProVideo Coalition; ASC new-products
key_findings: (search summary) Anamorphic traits: oval bokeh and horizontal streak flare; S35 Anamorphic/i = 2x squeeze, Full Frame Plus = 1.8x; lower squeeze weakens the characteristics; SF coating deliberately increases flare/aberrations
practical_applications: 'Anamorphic' in a prompt = oval bokeh + horizontal blue/amber streak flares + wide 2.39:1 feel; for 9:16 it fights the format
limitations: Manufacturer/marketing descriptions; qualitative

title: Why Do Anamorphic Bokeh Balls Look Like That?
authors: Haine C (No Film School), after Filmmaker IQ
key_findings: Anamorphic lens behaves like two lenses (horizontal and vertical FOV); out-of-focus highlights spread more vertically -> vertical ovals; needs the anamorphic element in front of the iris (front-anamorphic); rear-anamorphic zooms don't give it
Streak flares attributed to astigmatism
practical_applications: Prompt 'vertical oval bokeh' for anamorphic look; round bokeh = spherical
limitations: Practitioner explanation

title: Canon TS-E tilt-shift lenses (Canon Europe product pages; Wikipedia TS-E 45/50/90 entries)
key_findings: (search summary) Tilt rotates the plane of focus (Scheimpflug) -> wedge-shaped DOF: either an inclined subject sharp end to end or a thin slice ('miniature'); shift moves the image without moving the camera, keeping verticals parallel
TS-E 50mm f/2.8L Macro: ±8.5° tilt, ±12 mm shift, rotation ±90°; TS-E 135mm: ±10° tilt; manual focus only
practical_applications: Miniature look = tilt + high angle + saturated colour; architecture/storefront = shift (see lens_examples lens.shift_storefront_9x16, lens.tilt_shift_miniature)
limitations: Canon page returned 403 to fetch; specs from search summary

title: Laowa 24mm f/14 2x Macro Probe (retailer/review pages)
authors: Venus Optics (via Adorama, Imaging Resource, Fstoppers)
key_findings: (search summary) Long thin probe barrel, 85° angle of view, 2:1 macro to infinity, built-in LED ring light, covers FF and S35; 'bug-eye' perspective; Kickstarter-funded
practical_applications: 'Probe lens' prompt = wide-angle macro that travels between/inside objects (bug's-eye product fly-through)
limitations: Retail specs; no official Venus Optics page read
